lines.text: Here's a hundred-gigabyte file, and a laptop with sixteen gigabytes of memory.
lines.caption: Here's a 100 GB file, and a laptop with 16 GB of memory.

lines.text: Ask Python to sort it, and it runs out of memory.
lines.caption: Ask Python to sort it, and it runs out of memory.

lines.text: Ask the Unix sort command, and it just... finishes.
lines.caption: Ask the Unix sort command, and it just… finishes.

lines.text: While it works, files pile up in the temp folder, and then they vanish.
lines.caption: While it works, files pile up in the temp folder, and then they vanish.

lines.text: Those files are the whole trick.
lines.caption: Those files are the whole trick.

lines.text: This is how you compute on data that's bigger than your memory.
lines.caption: This is how you compute on data that's bigger than your memory.

lines.text: Picture memory as your desk, and the disk as a warehouse across town.
lines.caption: Picture memory as your desk, and the disk as a warehouse across town.

lines.text: The desk is small, but anything on it is instant. The warehouse holds everything, but every trip is slow.
lines.caption: The desk is small, but anything on it is instant. The warehouse holds everything, but every trip is slow.

lines.text: How slow? If reaching into memory took one second, a read from a fast SSD would take about fifteen minutes.
lines.caption: How slow? If reaching into memory took one second, a read from a fast SSD would take about fifteen minutes.

lines.text: A seek on a spinning hard drive: more than a day.
lines.caption: A seek on a spinning hard drive: more than a day.

lines.text: There's one saving grace. A trip costs about the same whether you bring back one item, or a whole crate.
lines.caption: There's one saving grace. A trip costs about the same whether you bring back one item, or a whole crate.

lines.text: So what matters isn't how many operations you do. It's how many trips you make.
lines.caption: So what matters isn't how many operations you do. It's how many trips you make.

lines.text: On paper, heapsort and merge sort are both N log N.
lines.caption: On paper, heapsort and merge sort are both N log N.

lines.text: But heapsort hops all over the file, and makes about four trips for every item it sorts.
lines.caption: But heapsort hops all over the file, and makes about four trips for every item it sorts.

lines.text: Merge sort sweeps through in long, straight lines, and needs dozens of times fewer.
lines.caption: Merge sort sweeps through in long, straight lines, and needs dozens of times fewer.

lines.text: And bigger crates only widen the gap.
lines.caption: And bigger crates only widen the gap.

lines.text: Computer scientists turned this into a model with three numbers.
lines.caption: Computer scientists turned this into a model with three numbers.

lines.text: N: how many items you have.
lines.caption: N: how many items you have.

lines.text: M: how many fit in memory.
lines.caption: M: how many fit in memory.

lines.text: B: how many come in one crate, called a block.
lines.caption: B: how many come in one crate, called a block.

lines.text: Then one bold simplification: computation is free. The only cost is the number of blocks moved between disk and memory.
lines.caption: Then one bold simplification: computation is free. The only cost is the number of blocks moved between disk and memory.

lines.text: Reading the whole file once costs N over B. That's our yardstick, and it's called a scan.
lines.caption: Reading the whole file once costs N over B. That's our yardstick, and it's called a scan.

lines.text: The classic algorithm is external merge sort, and it works in two phases.
lines.caption: The classic algorithm is external merge sort, and it works in two phases.

lines.text: Phase one: fill memory, sort it right there, which is free, and write it back to disk as a sorted chunk called a run.
lines.caption: Phase one: fill memory, sort it right there, which is free, and write it back to disk as a sorted chunk called a run.

lines.text: Repeat until you've been through the whole file.
lines.caption: Repeat until you've been through the whole file.

lines.text: It still isn't sorted, but now it's made of sorted runs.
lines.caption: It still isn't sorted, but now it's made of sorted runs.

lines.text: Every block was read once and written once: two scans.
lines.caption: Every block was read once and written once: two scans.

lines.text: Phase two: merge the runs.
lines.caption: Phase two: merge the runs.

lines.text: You already know how to merge two sorted lists: compare the fronts, take the smaller, repeat.
lines.caption: You already know how to merge two sorted lists: compare the fronts, take the smaller, repeat.

lines.text: Merge the runs in pairs, then pairs of pairs, until one is left, and every round reads and writes the whole file.
lines.caption: Merge the runs in pairs, then pairs of pairs, until one is left, and every round reads and writes the whole file.

lines.text: But look at memory while that happens.
lines.caption: But look at memory while that happens.

lines.text: To merge two runs, you only need the front block of each, plus one block for the output. The rest of the desk sits empty.
lines.caption: To merge two runs, you only need the front block of each, plus one block for the output. The rest of the desk sits empty.

lines.text: So use it. Give every run its own one-block buffer, and merge them all at once.
lines.caption: So use it. Give every run its own one-block buffer, and merge them all at once.

lines.text: A small heap tracks which run has the smallest item at its front.
lines.caption: A small heap tracks which run has the smallest item at its front.

lines.text: Move that item to the output buffer.
lines.caption: Move that item to the output buffer.

lines.text: When the output block fills, write it out in one trip.
lines.caption: When the output block fills, write it out in one trip.

lines.text: When an input buffer runs dry, fetch that run's next block.
lines.caption: When an input buffer runs dry, fetch that run's next block.

lines.text: Every block still makes exactly one trip in, and one trip out.
lines.caption: Every block still makes exactly one trip in, and one trip out.

lines.text: How many runs fit at once? About one per block of memory: M over B.
lines.caption: How many runs fit at once? About one per block of memory: M over B.

lines.text: With sixteen gigabytes of memory and one-megabyte blocks, that's over sixteen thousand runs, merged in a single pass.
lines.caption: With 16 GB of memory and 1 MB blocks, that's over 16,000 runs, merged in a single pass.

lines.text: So the number of passes is still a logarithm, but its base is M over B instead of two, and that base is enormous.
lines.caption: So the number of passes is still a logarithm, but its base is M over B instead of two, and that base is enormous.

lines.text: To sort ten terabytes on this laptop, two-way merging needs ten rounds over the data. The wide merge needs one.
lines.caption: To sort 10 TB on this laptop, two-way merging needs ten rounds over the data. The wide merge needs one.

lines.text: In fact, one pass to form runs plus one pass to merge can sort about a quarter of a petabyte.
lines.caption: In fact, one pass to form runs plus one pass to merge can sort about a quarter of a petabyte.

lines.text: And it's optimal: in nineteen eighty-eight, Aggarwal and Vitter proved that no comparison sort can do asymptotically fewer transfers.
lines.caption: And it's optimal: in 1988, Aggarwal and Vitter proved that no comparison sort can do asymptotically fewer transfers.

lines.text: In our simulation, that's the difference between almost a million trips, and about four thousand.
lines.caption: In our simulation, that's the difference between almost a million trips, and about four thousand.

lines.text: Once you know this pattern, you see it everywhere.
lines.caption: Once you know this pattern, you see it everywhere.

lines.text: When a database has to sort more rows than its memory budget, Postgress reports external merge, and spills runs to disk.
lines.caption: When a database has to sort more rows than its memory budget, Postgres reports external merge, and spills runs to disk.

lines.text: Big-data shuffles in MapReduce and Spark sort chunks, spill them, and merge.
lines.caption: Big-data shuffles in MapReduce and Spark sort chunks, spill them, and merge.

lines.text: Storage engines like Rocks D B write sorted files, and keep merging them in the background.
lines.caption: Storage engines like RocksDB write sorted files, and keep merging them in the background.

lines.text: Searching gets the same treatment: a B-tree gives each node hundreds of children, so any of a billion keys is three or four trips away.
lines.caption: Searching gets the same treatment: a B-tree gives each node hundreds of children, so any of a billion keys is three or four trips away.

lines.text: And the desk and warehouse are relative: the same model describes cache versus RAM, and GPU memory versus the rest of the machine.
lines.caption: And the desk and warehouse are relative: the same model describes cache versus RAM, and GPU memory versus the rest of the machine.

lines.text: So, when data outgrows memory: count trips, not operations.
lines.caption: So, when data outgrows memory: count trips, not operations.

lines.text: Stream through the data, instead of hopping around it.
lines.caption: Stream through the data, instead of hopping around it.

lines.text: Build runs as big as memory, then merge as many as memory allows.
lines.caption: Build runs as big as memory, then merge as many as memory allows.

lines.text: That's external merge sort: a logarithm with a huge base, which is why sorting a file bigger than your RAM usually takes just two passes.
lines.caption: That's external merge sort: a logarithm with a huge base, which is why sorting a file bigger than your RAM usually takes just two passes.
